segments.text: Modern (abstract) algebra studies structures — sets equipped with operations satisfying specific rules — rather than numbers alone, revealing that very different mathematical objects (numbers, matrices, symmetries, polynomials) often obey identical underlying patterns. This chapter builds from the most general structures (sets, relations) up through increasingly specific ones (groups, rings, fields, vector spaces), each adding more rules and, correspondingly, more usable structure.

items.text: Equivalence relations partition a set into equivalence classes; injective, surjective, and bijective mappings describe increasingly strict correspondence between two sets.

Groups (one operation: closure, associativity, identity, inverses) are the central structure of this chapter; Lagrange’s theorem (subgroup order divides group order) is a key structural constraint, and homomorphisms/isomorphisms compare group structures.

Rings, integral domains, and fields form a hierarchy of increasingly restrictive two-operation structures, distinguished by commutativity of multiplication, absence of zero divisors, and existence of multiplicative inverses.
Vector spaces generalise “vectors” far beyond physical arrows; basis and dimension are well-defined because every basis of a given space has the same size.

Matrices concretely represent linear transformations once a basis is fixed; determinants indicate invertibility and volume scaling, while eigenvalues/eigenvectors reveal a transformation’s fundamental scaling directions.
